---
title: "Pipeline notes: crew parallelism"
subtitle: "Reasoning and test results behind the terse comments in `_targets.R`"
date: 2026-08-05
---

Developer documentation for the pipeline itself, not website content. It is
deliberately **not** in the `project: render:` list in `_quarto.yml`, so no
project build touches it; read it as text, or render it by hand with
`quarto render targets.qmd`. Code chunks are `eval: false` throughout: they
record what was run, they are not meant to run again on render.

This file exists because the comments in `_targets.R` had to stay short. Section
numbers here are referenced from those comments.

## 1. What changed

Before: every triage PNG was written by one sequential target. 29 groups x 5
panels = 145 plots in a single `tar_target()`, on one core.

| File | Change |
|---|---|
| `.Rprofile` | Guarded `pkgload::load_all()` for crew workers |
| `_targets.R` | `packages` fix, memory settings, `crew_controller_local()` |
| `_targets.R` | `triage_group_slices` + `pattern = map()` on `triage_pilot_plots` |
| `R/fct_group_triage.R` | `triage_relaxed_cols()`, `triage_group_slice()`, `split_triage_data()` |
| `tests/testthat/test-fct_group_triage_slice.R` | New, 25 assertions |

Net effect: pipeline wall **175.6 s down to roughly 100-110 s**, using one fewer
worker, with all 145 PNGs byte-identical to before.

Three payoffs, and the second is probably the bigger one day to day:

1. Branches run concurrently.
2. Branches invalidate independently. Editing one plot function used to redraw
   all 145 PNGs; now it redraws only the groups it affects.
3. Each branch is sent ~1/8th of the data it used to be sent.

## 2. Why crew workers could not see `STOPAEP`

This is the part that blocks everything else, and neither obvious fix works.

crew workers are fresh R **processes**, not forks. `pkgload::load_all()` attaches
`STOPAEP` without ever installing it into a library, so a worker has no way to
reach it by default.

### Attempt 1: change nothing, just add a controller

```r
#| eval: false
tar_option_set(imports = "STOPAEP", controller = crew_controller_local(workers = 2))
```

Fails immediately:

```
could not find packages STOPAEP in library paths
```

`tar_option_set()` defaults `packages` to `.packages()` **evaluated at the moment
it is called**. The `library()` block at the top of `_targets.R` has already run,
and `load_all()` has already attached `STOPAEP`, so `"STOPAEP"` is captured into
the package list. Workers then try to `library(STOPAEP)` and there is nothing to
load.

### Attempt 2: drop it from `packages`, rely on `imports`

```r
#| eval: false
tar_option_set(
  imports = "STOPAEP",
  packages = setdiff(.packages(), "STOPAEP"),
  controller = crew_controller_local(workers = 2)
)
```

The pipeline now runs, branches genuinely land on a worker (worker pid differed
from the main pid), and every branch fails:

```
branch 1 pid 3476 -> MISSING: could not find function "triage_use_points"
branch 2 pid 3476 -> MISSING: could not find function "triage_use_points"
```

**`imports` governs hashing, not shipping.** It is what makes editing
`R/fct_*.R` invalidate targets (CLAUDE.md 2.2.2). It does not place those
functions on a worker. Globals in `envir` are sent to workers; objects living in
a package namespace are not.

### What actually works

Workers are launched with `--no-echo --no-restore --no-save`, and critically
**not** `--vanilla`, so they do read `.Rprofile`. They are also launched from the
project root, so it is *this* project's `.Rprofile`. Confirmed by having a branch
return its own `commandArgs()`:

```
C:\...\Rterm.exe || --no-echo || --no-restore || --no-save || -e ||
  crew::crew_worker(settings = list(url = "tcp://127.0.0.1:58565", ...),
  controller = "local", ...)
```

That gives both the hook and a reliable way to detect a worker:

```r
#| eval: false
if (any(grepl("crew::crew_worker", commandArgs(), fixed = TRUE))) {
  pkgload::load_all(quiet = TRUE)
}
```

The guard matters. Without it, `load_all()` would run in every R session started
in this directory, including the `tar_make()` process that already does it in
`_targets.R`, and including any session you would want to use to *fix* a package
that fails to parse.

### The rejected alternative

Installing `STOPAEP` properly (`R CMD INSTALL`) would also work and is arguably
more conventional. It was rejected because the failure mode is silent and nasty:
the main process hashes the `load_all()` version of a function while workers run
the *installed* version. Forget to reinstall after editing `R/fct_*.R` and the
plots are built from stale code with nothing marked outdated. The `.Rprofile`
route cannot drift, because workers always load from source.

## 3. Branching the plot target

Each branch is one group. Rather than sending every branch the full 90,110-row
table and letting it filter, the data is **sliced once** and each branch receives
only its own rows.

```r
#| eval: false
tar_target(
  name = triage_group_slices,
  command = split_triage_data(literature_analysis_ready, triage_pilot_groups),
  iteration = "list",
  memory = "persistent"   # see section 4
),

tar_target(
  name = triage_pilot_plots,
  command = write_triage_plots_for_group(
    data = triage_group_slices$data,
    grp = triage_group_slices$grp,
    ...
  ),
  pattern = map(triage_group_slices),
  format = "file"
)
```

### The slice has to be a superset, not the group

`write_triage_plots_for_group()` derives **three** subsets from its input, and
two of them deliberately reach outside the strict group (CLAUDE.md 4.4.0):

| Object | Matches on | Feeds |
|---|---|---|
| `group_data` | all 8 group columns | panels b, c, e |
| `group_data_all_units` | 7 cols, **unit relaxed** | panel a, dry vs wet weight |
| `group_data_all_geography` | 6 cols, **geography relaxed** | panel d, across site types |

So slicing to the strict group would be wrong, and **would not error**. Panels
(a) and (d) would render with a single unit and a single site type and still look
entirely plausible.

`triage_group_slice()` therefore matches on `triage_group_cols()` minus
`triage_relaxed_cols()`, i.e. compartment, sub-compartment, species group,
species, tissue. That is a superset of all three subsets.

**Why this needs no plot code changes.** `filter_to_group()` still runs inside
the plotting function, untouched. Filtering a superset with the same predicate
returns exactly the same rows as filtering the full table. Output is provably
unchanged; see section 5.

### Two traps avoided

**Do not slice in a branched target.** If the slicing target itself branches,
every branch receives the full table and the transfer has been moved, not
removed. `split_triage_data()` runs once, unbranched, and is consumed with
`iteration = "list"`.

**Do not zip two targets with `map()`.** Each list element carries its own `grp`,
so nothing has to assume two targets share an order. This matters because
`tar_group_by()` orders branches by the grouping column while
`sort_triage_groups()` orders the groups table hierarchically, and the two need
not agree. Pairing a group with another group's slice gives empty panels, not an
error. The earlier `tar_group_by()` / `triage_pilot_groups_split` approach was
dropped for exactly this reason.

### Downstream compatibility, checked

`tar_read(triage_pilot_plots)` still returns a flat character vector of all 145
paths, so the notebook is unaffected:

```
class: character
length: 145
all exist on disk: TRUE
membership check works: TRUE
```

One real difference: the vector is now **named** (`triage_pilot_plots_<hash>_1`
etc.) where `unlist(..., use.names = FALSE)` previously returned it unnamed. All
three consumers in `NBXX-Sample-Groups.qmd` use `p %in% plot_paths` membership
tests, which ignore names. Anything added later that indexes positionally or
pastes the vector into text should be aware of it.

The `tar_read()`-as-dependency-declaration rule (CLAUDE.md 4.4.2) is preserved:
the notebook still reads the target, not hand-built paths.

## 4. Worker count is bound by RAM, not cores

This machine reports **22 cores but only 15.5 GB of RAM**, and in practice
3-6 GB free. Cores are the wrong thing to size on.

Each worker costs roughly:

- ~0.5 GB for a full R process with this package stack (data.table, ggplot2,
  tidyverse, pointblank, eDataDRF)
- **65 MB for a copy of `literature_analysis_ready`, sent per branch** (90,110
  rows x 75 columns)
- an unbounded amount for `geom_smooth()`, which allocates heavily

`workers = 6` died mid-run:

```
✖ triage_pilot_plots_325c762a836da28b errored
Caused by error in `ggplot2::geom_smooth()`:
! Problem while computing stat.
Caused by error in `rowSums()`:
! 'R_Calloc' could not allocate memory (24826 of 16 bytes)
```

`workers = 3` completed all 29 branches, but Positron's R kernel then crashed
(`exit code -1073740791`) during a full `tar_make()` run. Not proven to be the
pipeline's fault, but the machine had ~3 GB free and a Positron session holding
data of its own is easily another 1-2 GB.

**`workers = 2` is what is committed**, together with two settings aimed at the
main process, which is the thing that actually ran out:

```r
#| eval: false
memory = "transient",      # drop target objects once nothing needs them
garbage_collection = TRUE, # gc() between targets
```

`memory = "transient"` costs some re-reading from the store. On a pipeline where
many targets depend on a 65 MB parent, that is a good trade.

### More workers made it slower

Counter-intuitive but measured. After slicing, at `workers = 3`:

| Measure | `workers = 2` | `workers = 3` |
|---|---|---|
| Aggregate branch seconds | 116.6 s | **197.0 s** |
| Pipeline wall | 98.2 s | 110.2 s |

The *aggregate* time going up is the tell. That is not scheduling overhead, it is
the branches themselves running slower because three R processes contend for
memory on a 15.5 GB machine. Cores are not the scarce resource.

**Do not raise `workers` on wall clock alone.** Re-measure aggregate branch
seconds; if that number rises, the extra worker is costing you.

### The `memory = "transient"` trap

`memory = "transient"` is right globally and wrong for `triage_group_slices`.
That object is ~243 MB in memory and is the dependency of all 29 branches, so
transient made the main process drop and re-read it once per branch. Dispatch
serialised, and the run came out *slower than sequential*:

| Configuration | Aggregate branch s | Pipeline wall |
|---|---|---|
| slices, transient | 154.0 s | 199 s |
| slices, `memory = "persistent"` | 116.6 s | **98.2 s** |

Hence the per-target override. The rule of thumb: a large object that every
branch depends on should be persistent, whatever the global default.

### Measured payoff, end to end

All at `workers = 2` unless noted, pipeline wall (not including the ~14 s R
startup):

| Configuration | Aggregate branch s | Pipeline wall |
|---|---|---|
| Full table per branch, `workers = 3` | 290.7 s | 175.6 s |
| Sliced, persistent, `workers = 2` | **117-137 s** | **98-111 s** |

**Roughly 1.6-1.8x faster using one fewer worker**, and the aggregate work
dropped by more than half.

::: {.callout-note}
## Run-to-run variance is about 15%

Two runs of the identical committed configuration gave 116.6 s / 98.2 s and
137.1 s / 111.3 s. This machine is shared with an IDE and whatever else is
open, so treat single measurements as indicative. The `workers = 3` result was
outside this band in both aggregate and wall, which is why it is treated as a
real effect rather than noise.
:::

The skew that used to set the floor is also gone. The slowest branch was 70.4 s
and is now 18.9 s, because that branch was dominated by receiving and filtering
65 MB rather than by drawing anything.

### Incremental rebuilds, which matter more

The headline speedup is modest. The invalidation win is not. Rebuilding three
branches after invalidating them:

```
✔ triage_pilot_plots completed [15.6s, 708.88 kB]
✔ ended pipeline [41.8s, 3 completed, 78 skipped]
```

Three groups redrawn, 26 skipped. Before branching, touching any plot function
redrew all 145 PNGs.

**PNG output is byte-identical on rebuild.** Verified: after rewriting three
branches, `tar_outdated()` still returns `character(0)`, so
`render_nbxx_sample_groups` did *not* go stale. Redrawing plots that do not
actually change will not trigger the 78 s notebook render.

### What the slice actually saves

```
full data:   90,110 rows, 64.8 MB
slice rows:  min 3, median 337, max 48,379

transfer per full run
  before : 29 x 64.8 MB = 1881 MB
  after  : sum of slices =  243 MB   (87% less)

worst single slice: 33.3 MB
```

The 243 MB of slices is stored as a target, but compresses to **8.9 MB on disk**
under `qs`.

## 5. How to re-run these checks

```bash
#| eval: false
# Pipeline is valid and branching resolves
Rscript -e "targets::tar_manifest(fields = c('name','pattern'), callr_function = NULL)"

# Build just the plots, timed
Rscript -e "t0 <- Sys.time(); targets::tar_make(names = c(triage_pilot_groups_split, triage_pilot_plots)); cat(difftime(Sys.time(), t0, units='secs'))"
```

```r
#| eval: false
# Unit tests for the slice. Seconds, synthetic fixtures, no target store.
pkgload::load_all(quiet = TRUE)
testthat::test_file("tests/testthat/test-fct_group_triage_slice.R")
```

```r
#| eval: false
# Per-branch timings. NOTE: tar_meta accumulates records from superseded branch
# definitions, so filter by time or you will sum two runs together. This caught
# me out once: 58 "branches" for a 29-group pipeline.
m <- targets::tar_meta(fields = c("name", "parent", "seconds", "time"))
b <- subset(m, parent %in% "triage_pilot_plots" & !is.na(seconds))
cur <- subset(b, time >= subset(m, name == "triage_group_slices")$time)
sum(cur$seconds)   # aggregate work; compare against pipeline wall
max(cur$seconds)   # critical path floor
```

### The check that actually matters

The slice is only safe if output is unchanged. Hash the PNGs, rebuild, compare:

```r
#| eval: false
p <- sort(unname(targets::tar_read(triage_pilot_plots)))
before <- vapply(p, function(f) as.character(tools::md5sum(f)), character(1))
# ... change something, tar_make(), then re-hash and compare
```

Verified byte-identical across all 145 PNGs after the slice refactor, and again
after the `memory = "persistent"` change. This works because `ragg` output is
deterministic; rebuilding unchanged plots does not even mark the notebook stale.

The warnings surfaced by this run (`pointblank` regex exceedances on
`PROTOCOL_ID` / `REFERENCE_ID` / `SAMPLE_ID`, unresolved (sub)compartments and
geographic features, `geom_bin2d()` dropped rows) are all **pre-existing and
upstream**. None of them are caused by crew.

## 6. Open items

- **Raising `workers` needs more RAM, not more cores.** 2 is the measured
  optimum on this machine. See section 4 before changing it.
- **The other two plot targets** (`triage_overview_plots`,
  `triage_species_plots`) are still unbranched. They now at least run
  concurrently with the pilot target. Same `tar_group_by()` treatment applies via
  their node tables; their key columns have not been checked.
